utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the Trial Chamber proposes that we deal with the matters in this way: We'll deal first with the outstanding matter of exhibits, and in that connection, it might be sensible to try and deal with them, as it were, chronologically and begin with the Cerkez motion, the Cerkez Defence motion, about additional materials. So you will deal with the Cerkez aspect. We then have, I think, the Prosecution rebuttal documents followed by the Kordic Defence Zagreb materials. We then have evidential matters; Witness AO and the tape are still outstanding. We have other matters, I think, about rejoinder which are not very long, and there's a motion about monitoring, as far as one of the accused is concerned. So if we can deal with the matters in that way. Unless anybody has any contrary submissions, we'll begin with the Cerkez motions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No contrary submissions, except that Mr. Lopez-Terres was -- I'd intended for him to deal with that. For some reason, he's not here, but he'll be here imminently and I'll hold the fort until he arrives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, are you asking us to take something else other than --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sure Mr. Lopez-Terres is prepared and he'll be down immediately. There must be a misunderstanding between him and me as to his immediate requirement here, my fault no doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we'll begin, then, with your additional materials which you've put in, and also your Zagreb materials. Now, we've got here schedules. We've got, in fact, a binder, but we've got schedules we can usefully look at of your additional materials. In relation to them, the Court has taken a fairly liberal view as far as the materials adduced on behalf of the Prosecution were concerned and also those adduced on behalf of your co-accused. As I recollect our rulings, the material was excluded if it wasn't translated or if it was illegible but otherwise, as I recollect, we broadly included all the material. It would seem right that the same rulings should apply as far as your material is concerned. In relation to Zagreb, you ask for two documents to be admitted, which seems modest enough. The Prosecution say that the second of those is part of a series, one of which we'd excluded under the Zagreb material earlier. But they say if there's a series -- one has already been admitted, you ask for another one to be admitted, and they want the third, which seems sensible enough. Is there anything more you want to say at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is my impression, that is to say, that the standard you mentioned in terms of the presentation of evidence by the Kordic Defence and the others, it all was reduced to technical things like illegibility, the nonexistence of translations. If I may say so, I made the criteria even stricter. We tried to avoid duplication. In the meantime, many documents were introduced that this Defence intended to tender in that way so that considerably abbreviated the proceedings. As for this second document from our submissions related to the Zagreb materials that you've just mentioned, I wish to say that the Prosecutor himself, during the disclosure procedure, disclosed that document to me, that is to say, Cerkez's letter from the 22nd of April, 1993 and also Cerkez's order releasing prisoners, because that comprises an entire entity of its own. I thought that it was necessary to introduce this letter, dated the 22nd of April, because it is only then that we have a whole, so to speak. I just think that I need to mention that six translations were missing when we originally handed in our materials and we provided them yesterday. We acted as fast as possible. Unfortunately, we were not in a position to do anything before that. There is no need for me to elaborate on any other matters unless somebody has questions for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sayers, is there anything you want to say about any of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, I think you were just coming into court when I said that it seemed right that the same rules should apply to the Cerkez Defence as applied to the Prosecution and the Kordic Defence as far as the additional evidence was concerned and, therefore, exclusion was limited to matters such as translations and illegibility. As far as the Zagreb materials are concerned, as I said, you say that there's one other document which you say fits into the series.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do apologise for not having come earlier. As for the Zagreb documents, I, indeed, think that it is important for the Trial Chamber to understand exactly the series of the 22nd of April. There are three documents in this series. Therefore, it seemed necessary to us for the Trial Chamber to admit all these documents together. It's the Cerkez's letter to Blaskic, Blaskic's letter to Kordic and, finally, the document written by Cerkez. As for the document that is being considered as an additional document, we have some comments related to the list provided by Mr. Kovacic. It seems that a large number of documents have already been admitted as Prosecution exhibits. There is even a document that the Defence has already submitted and that was accepted. Therefore, I think that this is simply a mistake, the fact that it is being required today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you a list --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you wish, I have a table of these documents. We have a list that was prepared and that is based on the request put forth by the Defence. It also includes our comments and it says here which documents were already admitted and, therefore, there is no need to have them readmitted, so to speak. Also, we have our own comments, namely that it seems that a large number of these documents have been in the possession of the Defence since 1999. They had at least partial access to the Zagreb archives when we, ourselves, did not have access to these archives at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, at this time, we're dealing with the additional exhibits, and what's happened in this case is at the end of the parties' case, additional exhibits have been submitted, and you will remember the Prosecution did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Whether it's in their possession or not is not a material matter. Could we have your table, if you have it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President. There is just one point I wish to make in addition to that. This is a document for which there is no translation. This is was supposed to be done by the Defence; however, we received this translation yesterday and we came to the conclusion that the Defence already submitted a document, that is D70/2 it has been admitted. This is the table, and I shall have copies of the table distributed straight away too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you a copy for the Defence, Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence will receive this document immediately. We have not received it from our staff yet, and I do apologise for this delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would seem sensible to put this aspect of the case back to allow the Defence to have some time for it. If documents have already been admitted, then there's no point in readmitting them. Mr. Kovacic, have a look at what the Prosecution have produced, if you can, this morning, and we'll come back to these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. President, I did expect the Office of the Prosecutor to submit this to me earlier. I even gave it to them in electronic form but, unfortunately, this has just not been the case. Just for the sake of the transcript, I wish to say one thing the Prosecutor says that the Defence, in their opinion, had access to the Zagreb archives. We state this quite clearly that in 1999 there were no Zagreb archives whatsoever; this is a result of our own investigation in Bosnia on the ground. A large number of documents that we introduced from day one actually are the result of these investigations in Bosnia in 1998 and 1999. Individuals, for one reason or the other, had copies of certain documents. As for the Zagreb archives, we got access to them after the Prosecutor did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. I'll hand this down to the legal officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll move on from there to the Prosecution documents. This is described as rebuttal documents. Again, we have a schedule of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May it please the Court. I also have an additional handout, basically a skeleton with a couple of attachments which may facilitate the most efficient presentation of this. May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, the Prosecution has tendered actually the number is now, in a sense, in some sense 35, because one of the documents that we were going to deal with that you will see in points 7 and 8 as an addition to our rebuttal list is a document which the Chamber has already now dealt with in the context of the Cerkez documents. That is the one document, if you will, that was, as I've said, here in my outline. We had the -- before that document was apparently admitted by the Chamber just now, we had a situation where we essentially had the bookends. We had the two end documents on each side, but we didn't have the book in the middle.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you slow down, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: ... that Blaskic had gone to Kordic for Kordic's views, but that's been resolved now. That leaves us, Your Honour, with 35 exhibits that have been tendered. In further reviews over the past couple of days, it appears that at least 15 have been admitted by comparison to the Defence's information, the Registry's information, and our information. In fact, as I mention here, there may have been --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just take it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I might also say that I owe the translation staff apologies for some days ago when, in one of the earlier arguments in an afternoon, apparently all of us were moving quite quickly, and my apologies. As I was mentioning, Your Honours, there may be one or two, or perhaps even more, additional documents already admitted that, in the course of further discussion this morning, we may resolve, but there was not complete agreement among the various records. Let me respond quickly to a procedural point raised by the Kordic Defence that some of the documents were not within the Court's deadline. It's our position that they were, Your Honours. Every document that we've listed and tendered to the Chamber now, or have tendered to the Chamber, is, in fact -- has, in fact, been listed and disclosed. I've just attached, simply to facilitate moving through this as quickly as possible, a filing that we made on the 13th of October, which is the second page of my handout where basically we just excerpted paragraph 10 of that, and we understood there to be a deadline of October 30. We made a preliminary listing earlier than that. The next document shows that on the 30th of October -- the 30 October deadline for various documents, and as the attachment will show, there was a further supplementation of that. Something like five or six documents were added. The point being, at the end of the day, Your Honours, it's our position that, in fact, all the documents that we've tendered have satisfied all the Chamber's deadlines. The only document that we had, in fact - which we admitted openly - had, in fact, offered after the deadline was the one document which the Chamber has now already dealt with. That leaves us, then, Your Honour, with 20 exhibits which we can go through and handle. Where the Chamber would wish, we could go through and I could identify which of the 15 by all of us, by the Registry's record, by the Defence and Prosecution records, which ones are already admitted if that's one way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us begin by doing that and seeing what remains after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, Exhibit 97, Z97, is admitted; Exhibit 367 has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Exhibit 141 was admitted yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, that takes care of that one. I'll just mark -- also change my list, Your Honour, as we go. Exhibit 141, then, has been admitted. I think what I'll do, Your Honour, if it's acceptable to the Chamber, is mention the ones as we go which -- there's some that might be admitted. For instance, 171.2 and 178.1, apparently, the Defence thinks that they've already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this is simple. If the Registry says it's admitted, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the Registry doesn't say it's admitted, it's not admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Let me go back, then, to my original plan, corrected, as the Chamber did, on 141.1. The next one where there appears to be no dispute on being admitted now is 367, 369, 394.1, 571.3, 595, 595.1, 595.2. The next document, Your Honour, was not properly listed. It was actually an attachment as part of 595.1. There is no separate Exhibit 595.2. Exhibit 603 was admitted; 601 was admitted; 609, 636, 714, 972, 1039.1, and 1335.2; based on further checking, Your Honours, those, further to our records and checks, were admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't have a 1335.2. 1356.2 was already admitted, apparently. 1289.3 is already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that leaves, as you say, about 15 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That leaves something less than 15, actually -- I'm sorry, something less than 20. Your Honour, we've also withdrawn a number of others of those -- we've tried to eliminate a few more in the last few days, which I think the chart notes in places "withdrawn." The first document not previously admitted and still outstanding, then, is 151.1, which we propose, again, for the purposes of the proper characterisation, in fact, of Herceg-Bosna and what it was. There's been continuing Defence positions throughout the Kordic Defence case of various characterisations of Herceg-Bosna as something other than a state or other than functioning as -- having functions and characteristics of a state. This document is further confirmation in response to the Defence positions of what it was. It was a united form of organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we can read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next document was withdrawn, 161.1. The next one outstanding, Your Honour, is 169.1. This was a document, as you can read here, and I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just give us in a sentence, what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In a sentence, Your Honour, the Defence case has raised issues concerning the Constitutional Court -- I can summarise the next couple of exhibits, Your Honour. The next series of exhibits, there's a few here, that all go to this point: As the Chamber now knows, there was a decision by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina which invalidated the declaration of the creation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and then subsequently there were similar court decisions about the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. The Defence took various positions through its case that this was not a valid decision, that there were procedural faults --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is to support the decision, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It all goes to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the next one --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The next one -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just look. I think you're right. 393.1, Your Honour, there has also been dispute throughout the Defence case as to the events in Central Bosnia in two respsects; one, what was and constitutes Central Bosnia, because there seems to be no agreement on that; secondly, the exact nature of the events in January 1993 and who started what. This document suggests that, in fact, Gornji Vakuf was clearly considered part of Central Bosnia; the events there were clearly relevant to what was happening in January of 1993 and what was happening, in fact -- that the HVO side began that offensive or aggression, consistent with, as the Prosecution will say, ultimata which were issued by the HVO side in early to mid-January. That's our position on 393.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The same, Your Honour, as to -- 421.2, to be clear, was not, in fact, proffered or was withdrawn. 449.1 is the same similar issue, Your Honour, as I just discussed. Same issue. The next one is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have a note that it's suggested this has already been excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That -- I think Your Honour is moving more quickly than me this morning. I apologise. That's correct, Your Honour. It was excluded at a prior time, but we believe that it is proper rebuttal evidence in response to the Defence's continuing issues raised in the Defence case. So it's true but, in our view, nonetheless, proper rebuttal. The next one then would be, I believe, 723.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The objection here is, apparently, to the effect that this was a -- as the Chamber knows with some of our witnesses, bundles of documents have been prepared in anticipation, and in the reality of things, not all documents would in fact be used for whatever reason, time constraints or what have you. The Defence takes the position that because this one document was part of an earlier bundle but not used, that somehow that's some sort of a waiver. We believe that it is proper rebuttal, again, on the issue of the respective positions of the parties in April of 1993 that, in fact, confirms the Prosecution position and rebuts the Defence position about who started what and the true nature of this conflict that, in fact, it was part of an overall Bosnian Croat plan to enforce its views of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. I'll just leave it at that. The Chamber's already dealt with 780.2. 815.1 was withdrawn. I think the next one is 1136.2. I'll just suffice it to say, Your Honour, that the Chamber's heard this in the context of the Zagreb documents, this is primarily tendered in rebuttal to positions taken about the relationships in association with the Bosnian Croats and Bosnian Serbs in Central Bosnia. A clear report by ECMM would talk about the close cooperation between the two groups in mid-1993. I'll leave it at that. The 1139.4 was a document releasing a witness -- excuse me, a detainee, Usonovic, from Kaonik saying -- stating that he was being released with Mr. Kordic's consent. The Defence objection there is that we had proposed to call this person as a witness and he was not one of the witnesses allowed. That's absolutely right, Your Honour. No -- nothing underhanded intended, but our position was the document speaks for itself without a witness and is proper rebuttal. Exhibit 1146.5, again, goes to Bosnian Croats -- my apology, Serb collusion in Central Bosnia and adds additional positions on that and also talks about the fact that the true managers of the conflict were in Zagreb and Belgrade respectively. Exhibit 1288.8 connects to the events in Vares, and it has been the Prosecution view and, of course, denied by the Defence that part of what was happening, indeed, most of what was happening in Vares and Stupni Do in the fall of 1993 was essentially what the Chamber may recall as reverse cleansing or self-cleansing when it was our view that it was part of the Croat plan to move Croat population out of areas that could no longer be admitted -- excuse me, defended or hard for them to continue to have -- to claim as part of the Croat territories under the various peace plans being proposed and therefore it was in their interest to increase the majority, Croat majority in other areas by moving Croat population from Vares, in this instance in the Vares area. That document goes to that. The next one is 1393.3. I might just say if I can -- the next three: 1393.3, 1473.13, 1473.14 all are simply legislation. They are sill simply parts of the Narodni List statutes related, again, to primarily legal matters. 1393.3, again, being specifically the decision invalidating or declaring illegal the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Again, I emphasise it's not cumulative or repetitious of the decision concerning the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This was a subsequent decision on the Republic of Herceg-Bosna and the findings of the Constitutional Court on that. Again, the other two final documents are simply copies of legislation. We withdrew, we've already withdrawn 2838. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, we've got your document setting the objections out. Unless there's anything you want to add to it arising from what's been said this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a few minutes, Mr. President. I'm not going to repeat everything that's in our documents. They speak for themselves. One point that I do want to emphasise though is that the Court instructed the Prosecution to file a final rebuttal list on the 13th of November -- sorry, 13th of October. We received a list but the Prosecution stated in that list that they had only listed some of their rebuttal exhibits. Well, that's not what they were ordered to do. They were ordered to list them all. So we prepared two tables, and I think that it's pretty self-explanatory. One is a set of objections and observations regarding whether exhibits are already admitted or have been withdrawn as were listed on the October 13th list, and then the second table states our objections to the new exhibits that the Prosecution has tried to add after October 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me see if I have the argument. As I understand it, the Prosecution are saying that they did, in fact, file all these documents by the 30th of October. Mr. Scott, have I understood that to be right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. There may be some apparently different views about various deadlines. We understood the deadline, the final deadline. There were various submissions along the way, but the deadline was the 30th of October. And that we complied with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you've provided here a copy, is this right, described as a list of Prosecution rebuttal exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And every document was on there except for the one that Mr. Lopez-Terres dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. So you are saying that these were the documents that were served on the 30th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it includes all of these documents that you're now relying on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is a problem with that, Mr. President, if I may. There are two sets of submissions which the Trial Chamber have permitted the Prosecution to make, and what the Prosecution is trying to do, very deftly, is to conflate those two. But there were two separate deadlines that were imposed by the Trial Chamber. The first was October 13th where we were supposed to receive a list of witnesses to be called in rebuttal and the exhibits to be listed in rebuttal, and we did receive a list of witnesses and a list of exhibits on the 13th of October. The second deadline that the Trial Chamber imposed, already been the subject of quite considerable litigation, was the deadline for Zagreb materials exhibits. The Court may even recall that we asked for all exhibits, including the Zagreb materials exhibits, to be delivered to us on the 30th, and the Trial Chamber said that it was not going to vary its earlier orders. So you permitted two sets of deliveries. One rebuttal exhibits on the 13th, and the second Zagreb materials exhibits on the 30th. What the Prosecution is trying to do is slide in a lot of exhibits, denominated rebuttal exhibits, that were actually delivered beyond the deadline that was imposed by the Trial Chamber. That's what happened, and that's why we've prepared two tables. One for the original list that was delivered as ordered, and one for the other exhibits that were delivered out of time. I might add, no application is made or was made for delivery of those exhibits out of time. Now, I just want to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to a few of these exhibits. I won't go through them all. The exhibit Z169.1 and Z169.2, these are two letters from the president of the Constitutional Court, Ismet Vasic, to the HDZ-BiH, the political party, not to the HZ HB, the actual party involved in the litigation. The Court has already observed that calling this witness would be reinforcing, in other words, simply reinforcing the Prosecution's case in chief and not proper for rebuttal. And our position is that any -- if the witness can't testify because he would be reinforcing, then certainly any documents that he authored would be similarly reinforcing. And I might say that the same objection goes for exhibit Z1139.4, but this is subject to two other objections. First, the Trial Chamber will recall in our opening statement we told the Bench that we were not going to be introducing any Kaonik evidence and we didn't. And yet here's Kaonik evidence that pops up by way of rebuttal. Well, it's not rebuttal. Also, there are some problems with the document. There's no stamp, and we contest the authenticity of the signature. That, I think, concludes what I have to say. Our specific objections are listed in the two tables that we provided to the Court last Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that I get the argument about the deadlines, you are saying that the order was rebuttal material, including witnesses and exhibits by the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course we can check this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Zagreb material, the 30th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And what you're saying is that the Prosecution are using the Zagreb order in order to get rebuttal evidence in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And I might say that we did receive a list of rebuttal exhibits on the 13th as ordered. But we received another list which we thought was the Zagreb materials on the 30th and then we received another revised package last Friday, on December 1st, and it's only become apparent to me as we've been having these arguments that many of the documents that were in the Zagreb materials submission are now incorporated into the December 1st submission. We tried as promptly as we could to prepare tables containing our objections to both of them showing what's in, what's out, what has been objected to as being provided out of time, and those have been filed in Court yesterday but delivered to the Prosecution on Saturday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So we have your note of the 30th of October material. Not all this is 30th of October material, some of it's earlier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's right. Some of it was delivered on the 13th as ordered, some of it wasn't and that's why we prepared two tables. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, the argument, and we'll hear your submissions about it, appears to be this: There is a distinction between the rebuttal and the Zagreb material. The rebuttal was ordered, we are told, by the 13th. We will have to look back because we don't have our orders in front of us. But we are told that that was ordered by the 13th. The Zagreb material was ordered by the 30th and we have already ruled on the Zagreb material. You are now asking us to rule on other material much of which was not introduced by the deadline it's said on the 13th of October. Therefore, say the Defence, it should not be admitted now. It is beyond the deadline. It's also -- it may be being submitted, I don't know whether this is the case or not, that some of this material we've already ruled on, but I may not be right about that when we ruled on the Zagreb material. Anyway, Mr. Scott, it's for you to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I will submit that there has to come a time when some of the personal remarks and personal hyperbole has to stop or has least be toned down. The accusation is that the Prosecution has deliberately, there's no other way to characterise counsel's remarks, that we have deliberately manipulated deadlines or tried to be underhanded in the submission of these documents. I categorically, on behalf of the entire team, I'm sure, deny that. We've been entirely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You needn't trouble about the personal comments. It's just the facts we want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me address those then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, could you please confine yourself, because we are not going to spend much time on this, could you confine yourself to specific documents. They are documents which have been admitted and the rulings of the Chamber regarding Zagreb documents. They are witnesses who came in rebuttal, and you say that in regard to these witnesses you have some documents. But you have to tell us whether these are the documents which are not part of the Zagreb documents and if they have to do with those witnesses. Please be as clear as possible, and we should not go back to a discussion which we already had, which is finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me answer -- finally answer both the President's question and your question, Judge Bennouna. Our position is - we've been, I think, very transparent about this in our filings all along, and that's why I've attached them in the handout that I've given to the Chamber this morning - that there were some submissions made and if we were incorrect, it is one thing to say we were incorrect, but that's different than saying that there's been some sleight of hand attempted. We've been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Chamber has not suggested any sleight of hand. Now, it doesn't matter what anybody else says. We want now the facts. We want to understand what your submissions are. Don't bother about what anybody else says, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. I'll go away from the timing question, then, to -- if I understand the Chamber's remaining questions. These are not -- it's a mischaracterisation to say that there has been some importation, if you will, of Zagreb material. The only Zagreb document that was admitted that, again, we were completely transparent about was 780.2, and the Chamber has resolved that this morning. We do not take the position, and we disagree with counsel, that the other documents that we've tendered and provided have been brought in after the Zagreb rulings by the Chamber. In fact, they couldn't have been because we listed them on the 30th of October, before any ruling on the Zagreb evidence, and they're already listed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. It's now submitted that you should have had them in on the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And our position, Your Honour, is -- I keep trying to answer that but apparently I'm not doing a very good job. It's our position, our understanding, Your Honour, that there were some submissions that were due as kind of progress reports. There are a series of submissions through the fall, starting at least on the 1st of September, various advance notices of the Prosecution rebuttal case and other evidence outstanding. It was our position -- the Chamber may rule that we were incorrect, but it was our understanding that there were some additional submissions due on the 13th, with final submissions due on the 30th of October, that included not only the Zagreb listing but also the final submissions on the rebuttal case. That is our understanding as the team. If we are incorrect, then we will be corrected, but that has been our position all along. It was stated in our papers. We didn't -- Mr. Sayers says we didn't make an application to put matters -- to submit matters out of time. We didn't believe they were out of time, Your Honour. We did not perceive any reason to make an application because we believed we were in full compliance with the Chamber's deadline. Again, as we stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, one of the points made by Mr. Sayers, as I understand it, is that some of the documents submitted by the 30th are exhibits which attach to rebuttal witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and which, therefore, should properly have been submitted by the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I believe they were, Your Honour. We've again been, I think, clear -- I think in my comments a moment ago, I readily admitted that, for instance, as an example -- I'll find my list again, Your Honour. One example was the release of the detainee -- it was 1139.4. Absolutely correct. It related to a rebuttal witness that -- it's not Zagreb evidence. It related to a rebuttal witness, and the Court, absolutely, no dispute, rejected the witness. We were aboveboard in simply suggesting that the document speaks for itself, and the document itself is still appropriate rebuttal evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must check on the previous rulings to see if there is any doubt about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And unless you've got anything else to add. Mr. Sayers, you've already had one go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I just wanted to refer the Trial Chamber to its ruling at page 25940, on October the 4th of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll check on that and we'll rule in due course. Now, we come next to the Kordic rejoinder and Zagreb material exhibits, and in this connection, we have the following documents: We've got a revised list of Zagreb materials and rejoinder exhibits, we've got the rejoinder notice of the 24th of November, and we've got a Prosecution response of the 29th of November. It may be convenient at the same time to deal with any submissions about rejoinder witnesses. Mr. Sayers, so we've got the position clear, you mentioned something yesterday, the rejoinder witnesses whom you propose to call, could you remind us, please, who they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. The first one is Zoran Maric; summary provided; estimate of time: Five minutes. The second is Jozo Sekic, former HVO president of Novi Travnik municipality; summary provided; estimate of time: Five minutes. We had hoped to produce Brigadier Nakic, but we have not been able to get in touch with him so we can't call him. Our third witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A confidential witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- has been identified in our papers previously filed. Estimate of time: One day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The rebuttal of those three witnesses, yes, I think you've dealt with that in your paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So you should be finished, if we start tomorrow morning, you will finish, presumably, Thursday morning, something in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you say a day, is that in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No. That's including -- I had actually assumed that this is a fairly significant witness who would be subject to quite a bit of cross-examination, and we were planning that his testimony should be concluded by the close of business on Thursday. I've previously cleared with Mr. Kovacic that he has, I believe, two rejoinder witnesses of his own, and he thinks that they will be very short and we can get through with them by close of business -- normal close of business on Friday, i.e., by lunchtime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Normal close of business for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. Is there anything more you want to say before we hear the objections to the material?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I deal with one of the witnesses, and then perhaps we can go into private session and Mr. Scott can deal with the confidential witness. As to the first witness, Zoran Maric, there is an interesting history of which the Chamber will want to be aware before it decides that it is proper for him to give evidence as a rebuttal witness and when, if it does so decide, it considers the scope of cross-examination. The Chamber will probably recall that on several occasions witnesses were called by the Defence, really, to put on either the whole of or very substantial parts of the Kordic case, and on every occasion, the Prosecution dealt with the witnesses very briefly in cross-examination, normally because there was a deadline -- a timetable deadline that everybody wanted us to keep or for some other reason. With this particular witness, as with several others of these large witnesses, there was a time deadline. It was a Friday. Your Honour wasn't sitting; Your Honour's two colleagues, Their Honours Judge Bennouna and Judge Robinson were sitting alone on this day. There was pressure to finish him on the Friday, which we did. On the Monday, I observed, Your Honour having returned, that there had been pressure - I wasn't objecting to that in any sense - but I certainly observed, because I thought it was important to do so, the substantial chunks of evidence that simply hadn't been capable of being cross-examined to. It's on the record for the 5th of June. Indeed, I simply wasn't able to cover with this witness, both as to substance and as to credibility, a large range of topics, including, as I set out, the entire second half of 1992, affidavits in support, his account for the start of the war, or what he'd said about Mr. Hadzimejlic, and those were only some of the topics that it wasn't possible to deal with. The Court will recall that this same witness featured next in the Zagreb document - it's been the subject of argument and has now been excluded - that related to and contained reports by four municipality presidents, he being one of those said to have been reporting within the document or said to have been reported by the makers of the document. The Court will remember that that document caused the Prosecution concern because they both wanted to serve it but they needed to make inquiries about it. Our concerns, as it subsequently emerged, I think, when Mr. Sayers said he actually had the document for a month or so, were, to some degree, misplaced; nevertheless, those were our concerns. The Chamber will recall that at the time of our formal service of this document on the Defence, we arranged ex parte to cover a day or so some immunity from knowledge of this document so far as Mr. Maric was concerned, and we did that because it occurred to us as highly possible that the Chamber might want him to be recalled by the Chamber so that he could be cross-examined on the content of that document. The ruling of the Court whereby he was not to be told of this document lasted for a period of time, and then the Defence asked for it to be lifted, and the Chamber, I think without calling on any argument, made the decision that it didn't wish to call the witness itself and lifted the ban on communication. Since then, the document of the four presidents was ruled on -- four municipality presidents was ruled on without the Chamber having any knowledge at that stage that it was the intention of the Prosecution to recall this witness. So that's the complex history for this particular witness. If he comes back simply to be dealt with in relation to one very small piece of rebuttal evidence; namely, a meeting about which there is some evidence, and I won't go into that in detail for the usual reasons, a meeting on the 15th, then, first of all, it will be simply to take further the unsatisfactory position of a witness being dealt with only for part of the totality of the evidence upon which he could be explored in cross-examination, and the Chamber may think that that is not satisfactory. If he is to come back, it may be that he should, indeed, be subject to broader cross-examination, including, of course, cross-examination on that document. For had things been ordered differently, there could have been no objection to his being cross-examined on that document, as, indeed, other witnesses have been cross-examined on documents said to be contemporaneous for their opinions, or for their evidence on the documents. Of course, it would have been desirable for him to have been confronted with that document without the opportunity to be prepared by Defence in respect of it, but in the way things have fallen out, that hasn't been possible. So that's our concern about that particular witness. Your Honour, the two resolutions may be, one, that the Chamber will say that in all the circumstances he shouldn't be called as a rebuttal witness and his limited evidence, so far limited because cross-examination could not be complete in the time, is where the position will end; alternatively, if he comes back, it must be on the clear understanding that he may be subject to more extensive cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I mean, are you asking us to exclude his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Whether he should be admitted is a matter for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So, first of all, I'm laying the history before you. Insofar as his evidence would deal with a matter arising in evidence we've recently heard that was otherwise not forecast, then prima facie he is a rejoinder witness. I accept that, of course. But it still remains a matter for the Trial Chamber's overall discretion what evidence it allows in, and in light of what I've said, the Chamber may be very concerned about having, as it were, two little bits from a witness when, in reality, it ought to have the whole of the witness. So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will be a matter for us to consider when we've heard what evidence he's called to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we can go into private session because it will be safer, and then I can also then deal with the next witness that I know Mr. Scott is going to deal with. If we can have a very short private session, I can be explicit without causing any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The matter we have to deal with next is the Kordic rebuttal documents. Yes. We now have the documents and we have a revised list of Zagreb materials. Is there anything you want to say before we hear any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Not really, Mr. President. We had originally listed 159 documents. We have withdrawn 46. Just for the Court's information, three of these documents will be authenticated probably through Mr. Maric tomorrow. There are 42 documents that will be authenticated by our confidential, currently confidential witness. I think, just by steady reference to the list that we've provided to the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber, many of these are in series. You have, for example, items 2 through 7, combat orders issued by the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone regarding Jajce tending to rebut the contention that the front lines there had been abandoned by the HVO. Item number 9 deals with a 1 million Deutschemark guaranteed loan to the HZ HB guaranteed by the deputy president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Hakija Turajlic in October of 1992, a month after the Constitutional Court decision tending to illustrate how seriously that decision was treated by the government itself. We have a variety of other orders, not all of the orders issued by Colonel Blaskic, I hasten to add to the Trial Chamber. There are many, many hundreds more orders than the ones we've selected here, but the ones that we've selected give a good -- they sort of round out, as it were, the orders that we've already filed and show the competence of the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone in doing things such as ordering the prison to be formed, appointing brigade commanders, and so forth. Just dealing, very broadly, with these exhibits, another category of exhibits are the ones that begin to appear on page 9. Many of these deal with the municipality of Vares, and I am bound to observe that, depending upon the Court's ruling regarding AO, many of these will be rendered redundant. If the Court keeps the testimony of Witness AO in the record, then many of these exhibits bear on issues which were addressed by that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it not going to be better to try and deal with this at a later stage? If 42 of the documents are coming in or 45 anyway, we have to make a ruling on Witness AO. The practicalities are that it may be easier to deal with this later rather than now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I entirely agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll deal with those that are left over after we've heard all the evidence. We'll put that matter back then which brings us to the evidence matters, two in particular: Witness AO and the audiotape. We begin with Witness AO. We have the renewed motion to strike. We do not have a response. Perhaps the best course would be to hear the Prosecution and then we'll hear you in response, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to that witness, I explained at an earlier stage that as between the choices of burdening the Chamber with more printed material or with an oral argument. I was minded to go for an oral argument. Although time has passed since then, I've stuck to that position. In our submission, the immediate reaction of Your Honour, speaking entirely for yourself, of course, that the matter should probably remain for final argument is the appropriate one. The position, historically, is as follows, apart from what you've seen in the Defence motion about disclosure. One observation to make about that, it should be borne in mind that the Prosecution has always taken its duties seriously all too easily, it could have been the case that it could have chosen to overlook further lines of inquiry that occurred to it when, for example, Mr. Naumovski asked certain questions of statements that the witness had made. We didn't do that. We've always been extremely conscientious even when it creates, as it were, embarrassing problems like this. So there can be no doubt about the conscientiousness of which we approach these tasks. AO left the Chamber having been cross-examined and as I recall, as I think I've informed the Chamber before, he was upset for I think two reasons. One, in fact, his name had been used in the course of cross-examination. It didn't, of course, come as a name to us on our screens because the writers always filter out names where a pseudonym has been given, and the Chamber may recall that I established with the newspapers and other media representatives that the name didn't leak out, in fact, publicly, so far as we know, beyond this building. Indeed, I was slightly taken to task by one of the journalists for saying that it was fortunate that that happened. They said it wasn't fortunate, they said it was because they did their job properly, and I stood suitably upbraided. But nevertheless, AO's name was mentioned. That was one of his reasons for, I think, disturbance and distress, and the other one was, like so many other witnesses, when matters are joined in the robust way that is appropriate to this system of being suggested that they are not telling the truth, that they don't much like it, wherever the truth lies. He left, and we subsequently discovered these other matters that had to be disclosed and of course were disclosed. The Court decided that he should come back for cross-examination, and it was our duty to do what we could to bring him here and we did everything possible. Ultimately, as the Chamber knows, the mechanism for compulsion lies with the Tribunal's officers, that is, the security officers in the field and, as far as I know, they've done whatever they can. Although the process by which they attempt to compel compulsion includes giving the people notice in advance so that they are always to some degree forearmed or forewarned. In any event, everything was done by those who had to do it and then at the last minute, for the reasons I gave on the last occasion, reasons apparently connected with or said to be connected with nonpayment of some expenses, he declined to attend. But I explained that, of course, that matter was always going to be resolved favorably to him if he was prepared to go through the bureaucracy. For whatever reason, then, he didn't respond and the Tribunal hasn't taken, I think, any further steps to deal with him for that. This Tribunal is different from domestic tribunals where, providing somebody can be located, he can be brought physically to court in short order and quickly. That doesn't happen here. The Chamber will also have in mind, in relation to this particular witness, that he is a Croat insider, to use the vernacular, and the Chamber will recognise how difficult it is for such witnesses to make a decision to cooperate and then to stick with it. Within the last month, you've had three examples of witnesses who were either initially highly cooperative or cooperative with the Prosecution and who, as soon as either they thought about it, in the case of one, it would appear, as his attitude changed; or, in the case of two of them, when they were approached by Defence counsel or representatives, their position changes. The Chamber's also had the recent experience in closed session of other types of pressure that can be brought to bear on Croat witnesses and potential witnesses. The atmosphere in the territory which can't, of course, be felt here, is a matter to be taken into consideration in all other dealings with witnesses. At the moment, it cannot be known what the real motivation for Witness AO's nonattendance is. One thing the Chamber can be sure of is that it doesn't relate to his having any knowledge of the matters about which he was to be cross-examined. The Chamber, I hope, will have noticed - I hope, indeed, that the Defence will have noticed even if it surprised them - that when witnesses are being brought back here, and I have in mind particularly Husic from America who was brought back through no fault of the Prosecution but because he hadn't been fully and properly cross-examined, he wasn't given any notice of what it was he was being brought back for. That's our complete and general policy: Nobody is informed so that the Defence can have every opportunity of dealing with the witness afresh. Witness AO was provided with absolutely no information as to why he was wanted back here to give evidence. Accordingly, there may be no reason. It may be cussedness. There may be bad reason, I suppose; there may be other reason why he is here. With that unresolved, in our respectful submission, the appropriate course to take with this witness is to allow, of course, all the materials that would have been put to him to go in and be available for argument and to take whatever approach the Chamber thinks is appropriate in those circumstances to his evidence, but for his evidence to remain as evidence before the Tribunal. To do otherwise would be wrong, in our respectful submission, he having given evidence and been cross-examined. Indeed, the Chamber will recall that in his evidence and, indeed, in one of the documents, I think, he makes it clear that he may have said other things on other occasions that weren't true, but he took the solemn declaration and gave the truth here. For our part, I make it quite plain, we won't be placing particularly heavy reliance on him and we will be approaching him with caution ourselves. But on matters of background, in particular, we may place more substantial reliance, we would wish to be able to refer to all his evidence, and it would be wrong, in our respectful submission, for him to be excised at this stage. Unless I can help you further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the testimony of this witness should be stricken for the reasons stated in our papers, and I have nothing to add beyond the chronology and reasons stated in those papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I understand the substance of the submissions that you have made, but I'm not sure that I quite understand this business of striking something from the record. I think you may ask that the evidence be disregarded totally or that no weight be attached to it, but I don't quite understand why it should be stricken from the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I confess to being a victim of the phraseology of the practice in my national jurisdiction. The functional equivalent of -- it really doesn't matter what it's called. We are asking that the evidence be disregarded. Whether it's stricken from the record or the Court merely says, as a result of the noncompliance with the previous directives issued by the Court and the fact that the Prosecution has had eight months to bring the witness here, whether it should be disregarded in its entirety, I absolutely agree. The functional equivalent is ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, will you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: ... I apologise for using the phrase that's particular to Virginia practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think I understand that much better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll turn to the audiotape. We've now had all the evidence about that, and we've got a submission from counsel for Mr. Kordic of today's date. It may be that we can look at it, or if you would like to say something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, that our submission says everything that needs to be said. It might be worth just reading it very briefly for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me just have a look. I've just looked at that. So that I can understand your position, Mr. Sayers, you're saying that you're not in a position to challenge the Prosecution's assertion that the tapes contain recordings of a conversation between Mr. Kordic and Colonel Blaskic. So as I understand it, and you say it's a perfectly proper thing to do, you're no longer, given the state of the evidence, challenging the authenticity of the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's a -- we're actually -- we have two positions, Mr. President. If I might just remind the Trial Chamber that we have previously submitted, on June the 7th of this year, a response to the Prosecution's report on what it referred to as audiotape handling of evidence. There's a problem, a serious problem, and I'm sure the Trial Chamber has it in mind, regarding the violation, we would argue, of Rule 81(C) in the removal of exhibits from the Registry. We have reiterated in our most recent submission that we stand by the arguments made in that pleading, but I felt that we owed a duty of candor to the Court to let the Court know that we are not in a position to challenge the Prosecution's argument that the conversation depicted on that recording apparently took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So I can understand it, then, you're not asking us to decide on admissibility, although you are asking us, of course, to decide on weight and interpretation and matters of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, we have previously made a request to have both of these tapes, 2801.1 and 2801.4, excluded for the reasons stated in our June the 7th papers. But the position was summarised yesterday by the Presiding Judge that we've taken -- we've made two arguments. One is that the conversation never occurred, and we're bound to recognise that we're not able to prove that, unfortunately. I did not want the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber to be labouring under the misapprehension that we would be promoting an argument that is devoid of evidence, and I have to recognise, in all candor to the Trial Chamber, that we don't have any evidence to challenge that. I wanted to make that plain and I wanted to make it in writing. But the characterisation of the conversation, the date of it, those are matters in dispute, as we've stated. The principal issue, really, is the handling of the evidence and that's the issue that we addressed in our June pleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what are you asking us to do at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We're asking for the relief that was stated in our June pleading, Your Honour, and I thought that the decision on that had been reserved, deferred, if you like, until all of the evidence was in. It appears that all of the evidence is now in, and so those issues have been fully ventilated between the parties and they are ripe for a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And you'll remind us of the relief which you seek.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: We sought, Your Honour, to have the tapes excluded. In the conclusion, we stated, on page 9 of our June pleading, that the integrity of proceedings could only be maintained if convictions are based upon proper evidence properly handled. This evidence, we would submit, for the reasons reviewed in this pleading, was not properly handled. The tape -- both tapes, both versions, appear to have been removed from the custody of the Tribunal for reasons given by the Prosecution but without the permission of the Trial Chamber, and that drew, appropriately, stern rebukes from the Trial Chamber. We basically stand upon our pleadings. I don't want to reiterate everything that's in the paper. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has all been dealt with fully in our own pleading of the 25th of May, I think. The matter is quite complicated historically but comes down, simply, to this: The tape that was actually produced by the witness Husic, the make of which he gave us the other day when he was giving evidence, was the tape that was relied upon, was the tape he said had been with him continuously from the time he made the recording, was the tape that was played, was the tape that stayed with the Registry ever since. It is the only Maxell - and that's the make of tape - containing these recordings and it has, in fact, been with the Registry from first to last. So whatever the procedural history and the alleged difficulties or even alleged improprieties, which are entirely challenged as a matter of fact, and on unchallenged evidence, the tape that's been relied upon is the tape produced by the witness. So the evidential position, dealing with things in the reverse order because witnesses have come in reverse order, the Chamber has heard live from the witness who heard the conversation live, recorded it and handed it on; it's heard live twice from the witness who processed that conversation and many others onto an original tape; it's heard how he himself copied that original tape; it has that first copy with it and that copy has been with the Registry from first to last. In those circumstances, there are simply no conceivable grounds for excluding this evidence which is clearly relevant, and in our respectful submission, this application must fail and the evidence must be admitted, subject, of course, to arguments thereafter about its value. Just finally, because it's important to do so, to deal with the history of the movements of the tapes in a couple of sentences. The Chamber will recall that there were two tapes produced or at least looked at in court. I'll just remind you of the history because it is quite detailed. Initially, a tape had been produced and produced to the technical booth, being the tape that had been transmitted by the witness Husic via his superiors to an investigator and Mr. Lopez-Terres, they having brought it to the Tribunal. That tape was the subject of cross-examination by Mr. Stein, who was trying to make a point out of the fact that the tape had been out of the witness' possession for the couple of days that it was with his superiors. Once that point was established, bad point though it may have been ultimately, the tape continuously with the witness was produced from his briefcase at the desk, handed straight to the booth, and it went to registry. Subsequently, those two tapes were listened to, I beg your pardon, a copy of the Maxell tape, that is a copy of the original tape held by the OTP, and the tape produced via the superiors and Mr. Lopez-Terres to the Court on the same day, were listened to by Mr. Stein. They had been retained in the possession of the Prosecution specifically to accommodate Mr. Stein. At that stage, both Mr. Stein and the OTP thought they were the two originals. They weren't. One was an original, one was a copy. They both then went to the evidence unit in accordance with normal practice in relation to original exhibits. They both then went without any subterfuge to a laboratory. They went to the laboratory because, as I've explained on an earlier occasion, it was expected that at some stage, the Defence were going to make or try to make some point about the integrity of the tape, and although we couldn't deal with it in advance, we wanted to know whether there was anything from a listening to the tapes that aroused suspicion that would have led to us take a different view in relation to them. That's what we did. The tapes then came back, and it all went to the Court. So, Your Honour, everything done to accommodate the Defence, everything done openly and, as it happens, the original tape has been with the Court from first to last. It's rather summarised it, but I hope that reminds the Court of an inevitably somewhat tangled history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll consider this and deal with the matter tomorrow, give a ruling, I should say. Now, that takes us on. Are we in a position to deal with the Cerkez Defence additional exhibits? Mr. Kovacic, have you had a chance to see what's been produced by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did, and I would just say a couple of words. I will not take time on that. It seems that the Prosecution claims that six or seven documents are already admitted. If so, and I cannot claim that for sure because they are very similar documents and relevant numbers should be also the original number on the document. So I suggest that either the registry or I, myself, can do that in the office. If they are admitted, of course, I don't insist to have the repetitive documents in the file. There is no sense on that. As per the other objections, there are basically four or five different objections, but related to what you actually said on the beginning of this session this morning when earlier, the Prosecution and, a little bit later, Kordic Defence introduced their documents directly to the files in the evidence, the only criteria was where technical areas, credibility and translations, if I am correct. It is -- that is because I believe that those objections or comments made by the Prosecution here entirely relevant. Because, for example, one of the objections is that the document could have been tendered earlier in the Defence case. It was up to me, because I was the last one in the row, to decide whether I will use certain document by certain witness or I should simply wait until my time comes. Because that was done by the Prosecution when they closed their case; they did it. When Kordic Defence closed their case, they did it, so I assume that I was entitled to the same procedure. As per other objections raised, for example, on the fact that document was a Defence exhibit in the Blaskic case so also could have been tendered earlier, it is practically the same answer on that because it was up to me to use that document at a certain time by certain witness or simply to put it in the files on the end of the case. I don't think that I have to take any further time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Scott, we've got your submissions here and unless there's anything you particularly want to add to them, we'll consider them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's Mr. Lopez-Terres dealing with this. Mr. Lopez-Terres, we've got your submissions. Unless there's anything you want to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. There is one additional motion which concerns the monitoring of phone calls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The senior legal officer has referred us to the detention regulations and Regulation 22: "Detainee may, at any time, request the President to reverse any decision of the registrar taken under Regulation 21," which deals with monitoring phone calls. So your route should be to the President, rather than the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm obliged for the Trial Chamber pointing that out to me, and we will take the appropriate steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's the senior legal officer, not the Trial Chamber. That deals with that matter. It remains to deal with the rejoinder for Mr. Cerkez and any other matters that anybody wants. We've had a notice, Mr. Kovacic, of I think three witnesses. Is it your intention to call them and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Kovacic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will, providing that we are allowed to, we will call the witnesses, Mr. Miskovic and Mr. Zuljevic. The subject of their testimony should be as briefly described in our motion from November 24th. Unfortunately, at this point of time, I am not able to confirm whether the third witness who is out of that category since that was -- it is an affidavit witness which the Court has ordered to be called for direct testimony. There seems to be some problems. I was not able to make telephone calls and I am planning to do that during the rest of the day so probably tomorrow I will know the status. I am informed that there are some problems, something like force majeure, but I will be in the position to advise about that tomorrow. However, first two witnesses I would like to call ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That will be on Friday or can you get them here earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I was trying to correlate with Kordic Defence and Prosecution, and there was a general consensus that probably we might start late part -- later part of Thursday or Friday morning. They are both relatively short, particularly the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from any other matters on Your Honours' agenda or list, there was one matter I was going to deal with about a potential exhibit called 351.2. Can I explain it with the assistance of the usher? It won't take me more than a minute or so. This is the communications register. It's not translated, and if it's to be admitted into evidence, I would ask that, for reasons of economy, it's not necessary to translate it and I'll explain why. The Chamber's heard of it from the witness Prelec, and with the usher's help I will explain exactly how it comes about. It involves looking, very rapidly, at about four documents. The problem arose with Exhibit 660.1. The original -- the English version I remind you of. And Your Honour will see, just to remind you of what the exhibit was, that it was apparently an exhibit dated the 15th of April going from Central Bosnia headquarters and relating to Muslim attacks. The next document is the original, as tendered in the Blaskic trial, of this document where we see that the date was not typed the 15th but was handwritten the 15th over something else. One also sees that above the date, there's no entry for the register number or whatever serial number of the document. That was explained in the Blaskic trial, I understand, is the work for some reason of those representing Blaskic in some way they apparently justified it. However, the original document was eventually available and indeed found in Zagreb and the same document for this is it, had on it the serial number at the top 01-4-508. We then turn and -- but if we can leave that on the ELMO for the time being, underneath the date and so on entries, you can see in B/C/S the topic that's referred to there. I'm not going to try and read it, but one can read it. The book that I'm concerned with, Z351.2, I hold it up is a very full slim lever-arched file, and at the relevant page, the entry for the letter of the 1st of April, I beg your pardon, the letter that has the reference number which we can see on the left-hand side, 01-4-508, is dated the 23rd of April, not the 15th. I'm very grateful to the usher. If you look at the block of typing to the left, you can see that the contents, even without being able to read and understand the language, appears to match so that that is the letter said to have gone out from Central Bosnia on the 23rd of April. This particular entry we have had translated, and by having this one translated, the column headings are described: Basic number, subject, received on, sender, and another mark on the right-hand side. And this is said to be a preparatory combat order for the defence of the city of Vitez although, of course, it was appearing in the Blaskic trial as a document showing Muslim aggression much earlier than the 23rd of April. Now, as to this particular document, that is, the exhibit itself, 661 -- thank you very much indeed for that -- the Exhibit itself, it was introduced by us through General Merdan, and he said of the particular passage "totally untrue". We now know, because Mr. Sayers acknowledged this in the course of discussions about this exhibit last week, that it's accepted by the Defence that the date is inaccurate and, to that extent, the document is or purports to be in its final state an untrue document. The point that was established, as Mr. Prelec told you, via this particular large, potential exhibit. Just to complete the history of documents with numbers, with references excised, there were other documents in the Blaskic trial at about the same time which also had their serial numbers excised. Why that may be is a matter of conjecture but, nevertheless, that was the case. This exhibit could prove useful to the Chamber if it found itself in respect of any particular documents and of its own motions or considerations wishing to check that a Central Bosnia Operative Zone document was recorded at the time and place when it should have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is a Zagreb document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a register.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which was found in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You didn't, I think, ask us to admit it or perhaps you did. I can't remember what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I raised it with you and said that we'd put it back and consider it when we had time to go through this little exercise, and that is how it's been left. Mr. Prelec referred to it as a potential exhibit and, again, for the saving of time, we didn't go through the exercise. He summarised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Prelec gave the evidence about it and the evidence about the other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About the particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The difficulty is that you're now introducing a very considerable -- potentially a very considerable volume of evidence in the last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It would be as I -- it would be a work of reference or something against which outgoing documents could be checked because we don't know, of course, how the Chamber is going to be doing its work or what issues will occur to it in due course. We can only, in a case with so much material, identify so many issues ourselves. We can recognise that this document might be something to which the parties would wish to turn. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I am being referred to our decision of the 1st of December which excluded that document 351.2. So we obviously considered it as part of the miscellaneous documents. It was no doubt attached to the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I think we had actually, at every stage, technically reserved our position, and the Chamber had agreed to consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will take it as if you had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We have enough evidence on the point. We think it's too late to introduce a document of this size. Now, any other business?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Order of speeches, I think, and timing of speeches next week was something that the Chamber was going to deal with and we now know it is going to be next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We'll deal with that and any other matters which anybody wants to raise? Anything you want to raise, Mr. Sayers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There is one thing, Mr. President. We had, in our papers that related to the anonymous documents, the brief that we filed on November 20th, there was an ancillary request made under the authority of paragraph 18 of the Tadic decision on hearsay in 1996 to exclude two documents Z1380.4 and Z1406.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The reasons are stated in the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You will have to remind us about it. Are these documents which have already been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: These are documents that we used during the cross-examination of Witness DL and Witness Zoran Maric. There is no corroboration anywhere else in the record for the statements contained in these, and both witnesses specifically disagreed with the contentions made in those documents. They are anonymously authored and frankly the same reasons undergird our opposition to those documents that undergirded the pleading that we filed on October 20th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We ruled on admissibility at the time about such reports. There was one, whether it was that one or not, was one subject of appeal. The distinction, Mr. Sayers, is that whatever was admitted during the course of the trial was one thing.
