But what we were specifically dealing with at the end with the Zagreb material was evidence being admitted right at the end, and you may have noticed that what we said in our decision was that it would now be impossible for the Defence to deal with it, "now" is the crucial word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm -- I am fully mindful of that, Mr. President, and I don't mean to revisit an old issue, but the reason that I mentioned paragraph 18 of the Tadic decision was, and just to remind the Trial Chamber of what it says, it says, subrule 89(D) -- actually, if I may just put this on the ELMO, everyone can read it and I don't have to burden the interpreters. The decision, and obviously it's a Trial Chamber decision, it's not an Appeals Chamber decision, but it's a decision that we urge the Court to follow. In the case of these two particular documents, once evidence has been admitted, it can later be excluded if it's shown to be unreliable and if it's substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. Now, one of these documents only, really, contains some fairly serious charges against Mr. Kordic. That's document Z1380.4. The other one contains some erroneous observations but they're, I'm bound to say, not particularly prejudicial to Mr. Kordic. The first one is, though, and there's no other evidence to support the contentions made in that particular document. And the same reasons that we've explored with respect to the other anonymous documents, in fact, that particular document, what we are requesting is, under Rule 89(D) and under the authority of the jurisprudence of the Tribunal as articulated in the Tadic hearsay decision, is for the Court to exclude those two particular documents, but most particularly Z1380.4, for the reasons that we've given in our pleadings. We have, I hope, comprehensively set out all of the evidence that relates to the particular contentions that are made in that document. There is no other evidence, I think, and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, that was omitted from our papers on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we are not going to change any previous rulings or any previous admission of documents. Of course, as was said in Tadic, a Chamber can reconsider a previous decision if there is some good reason for doing so, but here we can see no good reason. The argument is raised that, in excluding some Zagreb material, we said that it would be impossible for the -- would not be possible for the Defence to deal with the matters, but at that stage we were dealing with evidence which was being entered right at the very end of the trial, after the close of the Defence case. Other matters were being dealt with much earlier in the trial and there was the possibility then for the Defence to deal with it. So those rulings will not be altered. Now, can we deal with the next point, please. The next point is the order of speeches and timing and the like. We've got two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We're in Your Honours' hands. Yes, it's Thursday and Friday, or Thursday and such part of Friday as is available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long are you going to want? You'll have put, no doubt, a substantial brief in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to say, with a case of this size, there's no way one's going to be able to deal with it all in oral submissions. I haven't yet decided, frankly, what we're going to say in oral submissions. It comes for consideration after all the evidence is in, which is later in the week. We have got two cases to deal with. The Rules make provision not only for argument, but they make provision for rebuttal and rejoinder argument as well. That's what the Rules say. Those with North American -- yes. Those with North American experience who are used to the Prosecution having the last word, it's entirely a matter for the Court, I suppose, subject to the order -- is it 69 or 79? Let me find it. Yes, page 79 of the 2nd of August version, Rule 86: "Closing Arguments. The Prosecutor may present a rebuttal argument to which the defence may present a rejoinder."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're certainly not going to encourage that in the short time which is available. I would have thought that you will be able to deal with all the arguments in your final speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But, anyway, we haven't had an estimate yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. If there's a day and a half as opposed to two days, I'm not sure how much time there is available for us, does it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Friday afternoon will be available. That's in the next two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Given that we have two cases to meet and the Defence have one only each to defend, there's an argument for saying we should have approximately a day and they should have approximately half a day each. But I would try to finish in less than a day, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Kovacic's views on this are, Mr. President, but speaking for Mr. Kordic, it seems that the fair allocation of time is one-third, one-third, one-third. If there are two days available, by my calculation, that's nine hours. Three hours should certainly be sufficient to present our argument. What I would propose to do, if this is agreeable to the Trial Chamber, is just divide it up between members of our team. Mr. Smith would like to have a go on the persecution claim, I think, generally, and Mr. Naumovski and I will divide up in an equitable way the remaining claims made against our client, if that's acceptable to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I second the Kordic Defence's proposal. I think, yes, that it would be fair to grant each and every side a third of the time available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I also wish to say to the Defence and to the Prosecution is that it is not the length of time but the intensity of the argument, the intensity of the contents rather than time. There can be a question about the number of hours or the time allotted, but it really depends on the substance. The convincing power of whatever argument does not depend on the length of time. Everyone should be able to express himself properly. Evidently, the Prosecutor will say that they need more time insofar as the Prosecutor has two cases to deal with, whereas the Defence has one client each. That is one thing that one also needs to understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll consider the timetable. Now, are there any other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two very short points. One, there's been a continuing concern about the authoritative page references on transcripts. For purposes of our written arguments, what are the genuinely correct page numbers? What are the page numbers you will want us to be using, given that LiveNote and the hard copy have sometimes not coincided? I understand that that matter has been or is being resolved and that we will have or soon have a definitive list of what the page numbers are or a version with the page numbers. We will do our best in the time between now and 4.00 on Wednesday to ensure that our documents bear the authoritative figures. We can't guarantee getting it right in time because of the lack of coincidence over recent periods of time. The second thing is, if I may, there was something I meant to say in relation to the tape argument, if you'll indulge me with 30 seconds for two very short points; that is, as the Chamber will know in relation to Kordic's involvement in artillery matters, there is now, of course, further support for that in two of the exhibits, the diary and in the Exhibit 447.1 that's now before you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Anything anybody else wants to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Not from Mr. Kordic, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Not us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider these matters and deal with what we can tomorrow morning. We will sit at half past nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of December, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
